description: AgroRadar is a voice-first, Bangla decision-support app by Team AstroAlgo for NASA Space Apps Challange 2026. It uses NASA satellite data to help farmers choose profitable crop rotations against climate shifts. Farmers drop a pin to see rainfall and soil moisture changes over 25 years. The app speaks three picture-based options aloud, explaining the "Why" through satellite evidence and history.
summary: AgroRadar is a mobile decision-support app that helps Bangladeshi smallholder farmers plan their land around the problems of their own zone: drought, floods, and salinity. A farmer marks a field on a NASA satellite map. The app matches it to one of Bangladesh's 30 agro-ecological zones and builds a four-year, four-field crop rotation across the three seasons, Rabi, Kharif-1 and Kharif-2, adding mixed and relay crops for extra income. A multi-agent AI pipeline with explainable AI produces the plan, and an offline assistant explains every decision in Bangla or English, by text, voice or photo.
details:
Project: AgroRadar

Team Name: AstroAlgo
Challenge: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

1. What does it do and how does it work?

AgroRadar is a mobile-first, AI-powered decision-support tool designed to help smallholder farmers in Bangladesh navigate climate change and soil degradation.

How it works:

  • User Journey: The farmer uses a satellite map to mark the four corners of their land. The app automatically identifies which of Bangladesh's 30 Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) the land belongs to.
  • The Plan: It generates a dynamic 4-field × 4-year × 3-season crop rotation plan, incorporating mixed and relay cropping strategies.
  • The AI Assistant (AgroBot): Farmers can interact with the app via text, voice, or photo uploads in Bengali or English. AgroBot explains why a specific crop is recommended based on local data.
  • The Engine: Behind the scenes, a multi-agent pipeline processes historical NASA weather data, local soil data, and crop characteristics to generate a resilient farming plan.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Climate Resilience: By predicting weather anomalies and adapting crop rotations, it helps farmers survive floods, droughts, and rising salinity.
  • Soil Health: The rotation specifically includes nitrogen-fixing pulses, reducing the need for chemical fertilizers and restoring soil organic carbon.
  • Accessibility: A Bengali-first interface with voice and photo capabilities bridges the digital divide for low-literacy farmers.
  • Offline Capability: The proposed offline LLM ensures farmers can get advice even in remote areas with poor internet connectivity.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to protect the livelihoods of the 35+ million people employed in Bangladesh's agriculture sector. By shifting from a "one-size-fits-all" approach to hyper-localized, scientifically backed crop rotation, AgroRadar aims to increase crop yields, prevent soil degradation in the coastal and drought-prone zones, and ultimately secure food supply chains in the face of climate change.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Data Sources (NASA): NASA POWER (for 22+ agroclimatology features like solar irradiance, temperature, humidity, and root-zone wetness) and NASA GIBS (for Blue Marble and Landsat satellite imagery).
    • Agent 1: Explainable AI (XAI) feature analysis to identify the 9 most critical yield drivers.
    • Agent 2: XGBoost forecasting to predict weather conditions for the upcoming agricultural year.
    • Agent 3: Offline Large Language Model (LLM) to explain the rotation plans.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Multi-Agent Synergy: Instead of a single ML model, we designed an interconnected pipeline of three distinct AI agents (XAI, XGBoost, and Offline LLM) that collaborate to produce a localized plan and explain it.
  • Visualizing Time and Space: The app uses a 3D isometric grid to visually demonstrate how crops rotate across four fields over four years, making complex agronomy intuitive.
  • Multimodal AI: The integration of image and voice processing for the chatbot allows farmers to simply point a camera at a dying leaf or speak a question, removing literacy barriers.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Climate Extremes: We specifically modeled for the severe salinity issues in Zone 13 (Coastal) and the dry-season water shortages in Zone 3 (Teesta).
  • Socio-Economic Constraints: We considered the small farm sizes (1.29 acres average) and low digital literacy, designing a UI that relies heavily on icons, voice, and Bengali text.
  • Agronomic Rules: We integrated the NCTB Agriculture Studies curriculum and BARC guidelines to ensure the crop rotations are scientifically valid and culturally accepted.
  • Technical Constraints: We accounted for the lack of reliable internet in rural Bangladesh by architecting the final conversational agent (Agent 3) to run as an offline LLM, ensuring the app works in the field.
